lesson.title: The Subjunctive Door
lesson.subtitle: il faut que tu sois là, je veux que tu viennes — when necessity or desire crosses between two subjects.

hook.title: Stepping Through the Subjunctive Door: Il faut que & Je veux que
hook.content: When a wish (je veux que) or necessity (il faut que) crosses a que-bridge from one subject to a second subject, the verb after que steps into the Subjunctive Mood: Il faut que j'y aille ('I have to get going'), Il faut que ce soit prêt ('It has to be ready'), Je veux que tu viennes ('I want you to come')!

footnotes.title: Good news: for ALL regular -er verbs, singular subjunctive sounds 100% identical to the present tense!
footnotes.content: You only notice a special subjunctive form on a handful of core irregulars: être → soit, aller → aille, venir → vienne, faire → fasse!

pattern.title: Same Subject → Bare Infinitive; Two Different Subjects → que + Subjunctive
pattern.content: Use que + subjunctive whenever two different subjects are linked by vouloir or il faut.
pattern.linguist_note: French requires a finite que-clause in the subjunctive when the matrix and embedded subjects differ under volitional/necessity predicates.
pattern.trap_note: Never say *Je veux toi venir by copying English 'I want you to come' — always build a que-bridge: Je veux que tu viennes!

exercises.prompt: Match each subjunctive bridge phrase with its English meaning:

matching_pairs.english: Il faut que j'y aille (aller → aille)
matching_pairs.german: I have to get going (lit. It's needed that I go there)

matching_pairs.english: Il faut que ce soit bon (être → soit)
Je veux que tu viennes (venir → vienne)
matching_pairs.german: I want you to come (lit. that you come)

matching_pairs.english: Il faut que tu fasses attention (faire → fasse)

matching_pairs.german: I would like him to speak

exercises.target_answer: I have to get going (lit. It's needed that I go there), It has to be good, I want you to come (lit. that you come), You must pay attention, I would like him to speak
exercises.meaning: Il faut que j'y aille (aller → aille), Il faut que ce soit bon (être → soit), Je veux que tu viennes (venir → vienne), Il faut que tu fasses attention (faire → fasse), Je voudrais qu'il parle (regular -er = identical!)
exercises.explanation: Il faut que j'y aille ('I've got to go!') is one of the most common sentences in spoken French.

exercises.prompt: What is the literal word-for-word structure of 'Je veux que tu viennes avec moi'?
exercises.german: Je veux que tu viennes avec moi
exercises.natural: I want you to come with me
options: I want you coming with me
I want that you come with me
I want you to come with me
exercises.target_answer: I want that you come with me
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: I want that you come with me
exercises.explanation: Because 'I' and 'you' are two different people, French bridges them with que + subjunctive viennes!

exercises.prompt: How does a French speaker say 'I have to go / I've got to get going' using 'Il faut que'?
exercises.meaning: I have to go (lit. It is necessary that I go there)
exercises.explanation: After Il faut que, je vais becomes subjunctive j'aille: Il faut que j'y aille!

exercises.idea: I want you to come tonight (using Je veux que tu viennes ce soir)
cues: I want that → Je veux que
you come tonight (subjunctive) → tu viennes ce soir
idea_parts: subjunctive clause → tu viennes ce soir
exercises.target_answer: Je veux que tu viennes ce soir
exercises.meaning: I want you to come tonight
exercises.explanation: After Je veux que, tu viens steps into subjunctive tu viennes.

diagnosis.cue: After Je veux que, use subjunctive tu viennes.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Il faut que j'y aille maintenant
exercises.target_answer: Il faut que j'y aille maintenant
exercises.meaning: I have to get going now
exercises.explanation: Il faut que j'y aille is heard at the end of almost every French visit!
exercises.affirmation: You wrote Il faut que j'y aille maintenant cleanly.

summary.outcome: Use que + subjunctive (soit, aille, vienne, fasse, and regular -er verbs) after Il faut que and Je veux que.

use_example.german: Il est tard, il faut que j'y aille !
use_example.english: It's late, I've got to get going!

summary.takeaway: English 'I want you to [verb]' is ALWAYS French 'Je veux que tu [subjunctive]'.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([2703] Savoir vs Connaître): see how The Subjunctive Door leads directly into Savoir vs Connaître.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "I want you to come tonight" in French:
twist.target_answer: Je veux que tu viennes ce soir
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Je veux que tu viennes ce soir" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of The Subjunctive Door.

faut.english_meaning: is necessary (il faut: one must / it is needed)
faut.context_translation: We/you have to leave now (lit. It is necessary to leave).
faut.etymology_derivation: From Latin fallere 'to be lacking' — what is lacking is what is needed! Only ever used with il.

soit.context_phrase: Il faut que ce soit prêt.
soit.etymology_derivation: English borrowed this subjunctive twice: 'soit!' and the motto 'Honi soit qui mal y pense'.

que.context_phrase: Paris est plus grand que Lyon.

vouloir.etymology_derivation: Latin volō 'I want' → vouloir. A volunteer is the one who wants to do — the want-root English kept in voluntary, benevolent.

aller.context_translation: I'm going to go to the café.
aller.etymology_derivation: Latin ambulāre 'to walk' → ambler → aller. To go is a stroll away — and the near future rides on it.

faire.context_translation: What are you going to do?
faire.etymology_derivation: One French verb covers both 'do' and 'make' (like Spanish hacer and German machen).

venir.etymology_derivation: Prefix it to build a whole family: revenir (come back), devenir (become), prévenir (warn).

avoir.etymology_derivation: Latin habēre = have. The H dropped and stayed dropped — French never pronounces its Latin H.
